entities.summary:
Rudolf of Zähringen, born around 1130 in Freiburg im Breisgau, was a prominent ecclesiastical prince of the High Middle Ages, serving as the contested Archbishop of Mainz from 1160 to 1161 and later as the influential Prince-Bishop of Liège from 1167 until his death on the Third Crusade in 1191. The son of Conrad I, Duke of Zähringen, and Clemence of Luxembourg-Namur, Rudolf's career epitomized the complex entanglement of ducal dynastic ambition, imperial policy under Frederick Barbarossa, and the profound challenges of the Papal Schism that defined his era. His life's trajectory, marked by both high imperial favor and protracted local conflict, provides a vivid lens into the political and religious landscape of 12th-century Western Europe.

Rudolf's initial elevation to the Archbishopric of Mainz in 1160 was a direct consequence of Emperor Frederick I Barbarossa's efforts to assert imperial control over the church during the bitter Papal Schism, which saw rival popes Alexander III and Victor IV vying for supremacy. Barbarossa championed Rudolf's election against the candidate favored by Alexander III, Christian I of Buch. Despite imperial backing, Rudolf's tenure in Mainz was brief and largely ineffective, as Pope Alexander III refused to recognize his legitimacy and ultimately deposed him. Following this setback, Rudolf was appointed Prince-Bishop of Liège in 1167, a crucial imperial see in the Low Countries. His 24-year episcopate in Liège was characterized by persistent struggles to assert his temporal authority against powerful local nobility, notably Henry III, Duke of Brabant, and the burgeoning burgher class. He engaged in numerous military campaigns to defend and expand the Prince-Bishopric's territories, transforming the see into a formidable temporal power.
